mappings.note: Invent your own star pattern and a story for it, then compare with others'. LO-142 is creativity in designing and planning; no content LO covers making up an asterism.
Go out, find the Big Dipper, then follow its pointers five lengths to the Pole Star. A field observation carried out to answer a query, LO-134.
Find Orion, then extend the belt line east to Sirius. A conducted sky observation, LO-134.
Look for Venus at dusk and again before dawn, and view the sky through a telescope. Observation with an instrument, LO-134.
Solve the letter riddle for MARS, then WRITE TWO MORE. The composing half is the student's own invention, LO-142.
Which is not a Solar System member -- Sirius, a star outside it. Sorting bodies into the Solar System and beyond, LO-133.
Which is not a planet -- Pluto, reclassified as a dwarf planet. Tests the boundary of the planet class, LO-133.
Which is brighter, the Pole Star or Sirius. An explicit comparison of two objects on an observable property, LO-132.
Check the artist's Solar System figure and write the correct planet order into the boxes. Correcting a labelled diagram, LO-138.
Draw lines joining the stars of the Big and Little Dippers and label the Pole Star. Producing a labelled diagram, LO-138.
Draw the lines for Orion and label Sirius. Producing a labelled diagram, LO-138. The printed answer is the next item's stem.
Why stars are invisible by day -- sunlight scatters and overpowers them. The item asks for the cause, LO-135.
Observe the Big Dipper three or four times through one night and SKETCH its positions with times. LO-134 for the timed repeated observation, LO-138 for the required sketch.
Write a poem or story about the night sky. Creative work with no content outcome to hold it, LO-142.
What a constellation is -- a group of stars forming a recognisable pattern. Defining a class of sky object, LO-133.
Sirius is the brightest star, in Canis Major. Identifying an object by an observable feature, LO-131.
Why star patterns mattered to sailors and travellers -- finding directions. LO-140's register of applying learning in daily life, the same one that names the compass.
The IAU divides the sky into 88 constellations. The formal classification of the whole sky, LO-133.
The hunter with three belt stars is Orion. Identification by an observable pattern, LO-131.

What causes light pollution -- excess artificial light with smoke and dust. Cited at LO-141 because light pollution is an environmental harm the chapter asks students to recognise; the frame has no LO for it.
The pointer-star method for locating Polaris. A procedure for a field observation, LO-134.
The key difference between the Sun and other stars as seen from Earth. An explicit differentiation, LO-132.
What the Sun is -- a hot spherical ball of gases making its own light. Identification by observable features, LO-131.
The Sun is about 150 million km away, which defines one astronomical unit. A physical quantity with its unit, LO-137.
Why other stars look like points -- they are vastly farther away. The cause of an appearance, LO-135.
What a planet is. Defining a class of body, LO-133.
Mars is the Red Planet, from its reddish soil. Identification by appearance, LO-131.
How the inner four planets DIFFER from the outer four. An explicit differentiation on size and structure, LO-132.
Which is NOT one of the eight planets -- Pluto. Tests the boundary of the planet class, LO-133.
The bright dawn object near the eastern horizon is Venus. Identification from where and when it appears, LO-131.
How to tell a planet from a star by eye -- stars twinkle, planets do not. A differentiation on an observable property, LO-132.
Natural satellites of planets are moons. Naming a class of body, LO-131.
The Moon orbits Earth in about 27 days. A measured period, LO-137.
Lunar craters and how impacts formed them. The item names the feature AND asks how it arose, so the cause, LO-135.
Assertion-reason: stars shine with their own light BECAUSE they are hot gas balls producing energy. The causal clause is what is marked, LO-135.
Which bodies make up the Solar System -- the Sun, planets, moons, plus comets and asteroids. Populating the class, LO-133. The stem retains only the last of the three numbered items.
What a telescope does -- gathers more light so faint, distant objects show detail. The instrument that makes the chapter's observations possible, LO-134.
Chandrayaan-1, India's first Moon mission of 2008. Space exploration applied; the frame has no LO for missions, and LO-140 is the nearest honest fit for science put to use.
What asteroids are -- small, rocky, irregular bodies between Mars and Jupiter. Identification by observable features, LO-131.
Why a comet grows a tail near the Sun -- its ice vaporises. The item asks for the cause, LO-135.
Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years. A measured period, LO-137.
What the Milky Way is -- the galaxy containing our Solar System. Placing our system within a larger class, LO-133.
Stars make their own light, planets reflect it. An explicit differentiation on a defining property, LO-132.
Which is NOT why Nubra's sky is clear -- artificial lights. Recognising light and air pollution as what spoils a sky, LO-141.
Assertion-reason: Polaris looks fixed BECAUSE it sits near the extended axis of rotation. The causal clause is what is marked, LO-135.
Which night and place give the best view of a faint constellation. Planning the conditions of an observation, LO-134.
Nakshatra denotes a star or a small group of them, such as Ardra or Krittika. An Indian classification of sky objects, LO-133.
Why to dark-adapt for half an hour before sky watching. Preparing properly for an observation, LO-134.
Motion of one body around a larger one is revolution. Naming a process, LO-136.
Earth's natural satellite is the Moon. Naming a body, LO-131.
How Earth's surface differs from the Moon's in atmosphere and life. An explicit differentiation of two bodies, LO-132.
Which is not an inner planet -- Jupiter. Sorting planets into inner and outer groups, LO-133.

A planet orbiting another star is an exoplanet. Extending the planet classification beyond our system, LO-133; NEP content the frame does not anticipate. The term is corrupted to 'explanted' in the options.
Nubra, Ladakh, prized for clear skies and low pollution. The narrative setting, tied to the chapter's point about pollution-free skies, LO-141.
Why massive stars look like points -- extreme distance. The cause of an appearance, LO-135.
Earth's motion around the Sun is revolution. Naming a process, LO-136.
Venus is the Morning and Evening Star. Identification by when and where it is seen, LO-131.
The structural difference between inner rocky and outer gaseous planets. An explicit differentiation, LO-132.
Which is NOT an asteroid feature -- a long tail, which belongs to comets. Requires holding asteroids and comets apart on their properties, LO-132.
What to look for first when hunting Orion -- the three belt stars. The practical method of a field observation, LO-134.
